Aerospace · Team project · Spring 2025

Predicting a rocket's flight before it flies

I created the full rocket CAD model in SolidWorks using the LOC-IV airframe as the reference, then connected the geometry to aerodynamic and flight analysis. I developed the CFD study, OpenRocket model and plots to examine how the rocket’s shape and propulsion affect its predicted flight.

  • SolidWorks
  • SolidWorks Flow Simulation
  • OpenRocket
  • Thrust-curve modeling

My roleCAD geometry in SolidWorks, SolidWorks CFD pressure and velocity studies, the drag analysis, the OpenRocket flight simulation and all of the plots. Airframe fabrication, electronics and launch operations were handled by teammates.

Workflowmodel → fly → compare
Exact CAD replica of the LOC-IV airframe in SolidWorks
CFD pressure and velocity cut plots across the expected speed range
Pressure forces reduced to a drag coefficient vs. velocity
OpenRocket run on the H100 DMS thrust curve for apogee, max velocity, time to apogee
≈0.38Cd plateau, 10–150 m/s
150 m/stop of CFD velocity sweep
H100Aerotech DMS thrust curve

Aerodynamics

SolidWorks CFD resolved the pressure and velocity fields around the rocket geometry. I used surface-pressure data to study drag across the expected velocity range. The drag coefficient settles near 0.38 above about 10 m/s, after a low-speed peak near 0.41. Pressure drag is only part of the total, since skin friction adds to it.

Flight prediction

OpenRocket used the Aerotech H100 DMS thrust curve as the propulsion input and estimated altitude, velocity and time to apogee. Together these define the predicted flight envelope and give a baseline for comparing against flight measurements.

Reading them together

OpenRocket describes the overall flight profile; CFD shows the local flow and loading behind it. Reading the two together connects the predicted trajectory to the forces that explain it.

Robotics · Original design · Creo

4-DOF robotic arm with a three-prong gripper

I designed this desktop robotic arm in Creo, from the bearing-supported base and articulated links to the gear-coupled three-prong gripper. The mechanism combines base yaw, shoulder, elbow and wrist pitch with a powered claw. I created 22 unique structural and gripper parts and organized the full assembly into seven rigid subassemblies.

  • Creo Parametric
  • Gear-coupled gripper
  • Bearing-supported yaw
  • Static torque screening
  • Clearance sweeps
  • PETG / TPU

The base carries the yaw axis on a 6806 bearing (30 × 42 × 7 mm) through a printed spindle with M3 heat-set inserts, so the arm's moment goes into the bearing instead of the servo shaft. Two DS3225 servos drive shoulder and elbow, DS3218s drive yaw and wrist, and an MG90D runs the claw. Links are 100 mm (upper) and 80 mm (fore) with a 60 mm palm.

In the second revision I replaced the two-finger claw with a three-prong hand. The thumb sits centered between two 5 mm tines that bolt to a separate drive gear, so all three prongs move from one servo through one meshed gear pair. Splitting the fork into flat-printed tines removed the supports a one-piece fork needed and made the fingers replaceable.

Torque screening

Shoulder4.91 kgf·cm · 4.3× stall-torque ratio
Elbow2.10 kgf·cm · 10.0× stall-torque ratio
Wrist0.69 kgf·cm · 26.2× stall-torque ratio

Worst case: every link horizontal with a 25 g object, 100% solid PETG masses and a 10% hardware allowance, against the servos' catalog stall torque. These ratios are preliminary sizing checks, not continuous-duty safety factors; thermal and dynamic loads require separate validation.

Clearance checks

Eight arm poses across the joint ranges show no printed-part intersections above 0.005 mm³, including against the servo, bearing and fastener envelopes. The hand was swept 0–35° in 1° steps (36 positions) with no collisions; the closest pad-to-pad gap is 2.12 mm.

Design for assembly

I designed the links, servo interfaces and gripper as replaceable components, with accessible fasteners and flat mounting faces. PETG structural parts carry the loads, while TPU fingertip pads provide compliance at the contact surface. Separate fork tines simplify fabrication and allow a damaged finger to be replaced without rebuilding the hand.

6-DOF robotic arm, from CAD assembly to the shop floor

A desktop robot arm with five positioning axes and a gripper, driven by six Feetech STS3215 bus servos. I built it on the open-source SO-101 platform: I assembled and mated the full design in FreeCAD, defined every joint axis, redesigned the base retainer and controller mount, ran a full interference audit and wrote the bill of materials. I'm fabricating it now.

  • FreeCAD 1.0.2
  • Parametric Part Design
  • Assembly mates
  • Forward & inverse kinematics
  • Interference analysis
  • DFM for FDM printing
  • BOM

Base design: SO-101 by TheRobotStudio (Apache-2.0). The modifications, assembly and analysis below are mine.

Live kinematics · side viewdrag the gripper ✥
0°
0°
0°
0°

Kinematic chain

Seven rigid groups (base, shoulder, upper arm, forearm, wrist, gripper, moving jaw) connected by six revolute joints. Each joint is a datum point and unit axis in the assembly frame. I kept the real axes instead of snapping them to the global axes: the base yaw axis sits 0.5° off vertical in the source geometry, and forcing it straight would misplace every link downstream.

Forward kinematics

I wrote a FreeCAD pose-control macro that builds each group's placement by composing rotations about every parent joint's axis through its pivot, from the base outward, then runs the native assembly solver. A combined test pose (±2.5° on all six joints) preserved joint-center alignment to numerical solver precision and returned the assembly to its home pose. This checks the CAD transformation, not physical positioning accuracy.

Inverse kinematics

Shoulder, elbow and wrist pitch form a planar chain with 116.1 mm and 134.2 mm links. Given a gripper target, I subtract the fixed wrist offset, solve the two-link triangle with the law of cosines (elbow-up branch), then set wrist pitch to −(θ₂+θ₃) so the gripper keeps its orientation. That is the solver running in the demo above.

Controller mount, rebuilt parametrically

Rebuilt from four fully constrained sketches with real pad, pocket, fillet and chamfer features: a 51 × 42 × 4 mm plate with R7 corners, a 37 × 28 mm board pattern of Ø3.3 holes, two Ø8 seating lands 0.298 mm proud, and 90° Ø6.2 countersinks so M3 flat-head screws sit flush. Feature depths are linked by expressions, and I tested it by flexing thickness 4 → 4.2 mm and width 51 → 52 mm and back with a valid solid every time.

Base motor retainer

Added clearance relief at the base and two captured M3 nuts so the controller plate bolts on with two M3 × 10 flat-heads. Behind the board holes I specified threaded spacers instead of nuts, because the retainer blocks that space.

Interference audit

All 55 printed-part pairs are clear (no overlap above 0.01 mm³) in the home pose. Checking printed parts against the servo models flagged 26 overlaps, the largest about 657.5 mm³ at the upper-arm elbow servo. I'm reconciling those against the STS3215 drawings and fit-checking printed joints before committing the full print.

Robotics · Personal project · Bipedal legs

10-DOF bipedal robot legs

I created and designed this 10-DOF bipedal leg assembly in SolidWorks, including the pelvis, servo cartridges, leg links, ankle supports and feet. Each leg has hip roll, hip pitch, knee, ankle pitch and ankle roll. The 420 mm assembly uses ten ST3215 12 V servos, with 96 mm between foot centers and 89 mm between pitch axes.

  • SolidWorks
  • Assembly mates
  • URDF kinematics
  • Constraint solving
  • PETG + TPU

Every joint uses the same servo cartridge: a printed saddle and cap hold the servo, two cheeks bolt to the metal drive horn and the passive rear horn, and a bolted bridge ties them into a fork. The output is supported on both sides, so bending loads don't sit on the servo shaft alone. Structural joints use captive nuts and through-bolts instead of screws threaded into plastic.

The feet are rigid 110 × 78 mm PETG plates with a 5 mm base, an 8 mm ankle boss and ribs that carry load straight from the ankle into the base, with a bolted 4 mm TPU traction sole whose screw heads sit 0.5 mm above the tread.

Crouch & weight shiftside + front views
0°
0°

Kinematics

Joint heights at neutral are 359, 290, 201, 112 and 43 mm. A crouch couples hip −θ, knee +2θ and ankle −θ so the feet stay flat. A sideways weight shift pairs equal hip roll with opposite ankle roll so the feet stay level while the pelvis moves over the support foot. The assembly preserves ten revolute degrees of freedom. The coordinated poses demonstrate the intended motion, not a validated walking gait.

Torque budget

ST3215 12 V: 0.98 N·m rated, 2.94 N·m stall. For a 1.5 kg scenario, static torque is m·g·r: 0.29 N·m at a 20 mm lever arm (30% of rated) up to 0.88 N·m at 60 mm (90%). Shifting onto one foot without first moving the center of mass uses most of the margin, so weight shift has to come before foot lift.

Checks

I checked the assembly for interference in neutral, crouch (12/24/12°) and ±4° roll poses. The joint layout preserves ten revolute degrees of freedom. These checks evaluate mechanical clearance and articulation; walking stability still requires physical testing and balance-control development.

Mechatronics · Personal project · Embedded

Metal-detecting rover

I designed the rover chassis, motor mounts, adjustable sensor boom and coil housing in SolidWorks, integrating the mechanical assembly with Arduino control and Bluetooth communication. A 100 mm search coil sits about 16 cm ahead of the chassis to separate the sensing area from the drive hardware. The control system combines remote driving, automatic patrol and a stop-and-alert response to metal detection.

  • SolidWorks assembly
  • Arduino C++
  • Pulse induction
  • MOSFET driver
  • Input capture timing
  • HC-05 Bluetooth

The detector pulses the coil through an IRF740 400 V MOSFET driven by a TC4420 gate driver. When the pulse ends, the coil's flyback spikes to roughly 300 V and decays. An LM393 comparator stays high while the decay is above a threshold, and the Arduino's Timer1 input capture measures that high time to 62.5 ns. Metal under the coil holds eddy currents that stretch the decay, so a longer high time means a find.

Both comparator inputs come from dividers on the same battery rail, so battery sag shifts the signal and the threshold together and the threshold doesn't drift as the cells drain.

How detection works
Pulse 50 µs every 2 msAveraged 32 pulses ≈ 64 msTrigger +3 ticks = 187.5 ns

Waveform is illustrative, not a scope capture.

Firmware

At power-up it averages 40 readings over about 2.5 s to set a baseline and noise level, then slowly tracks drift (α = 0.002) only while no metal is present. A rise of 3 ticks over baseline triggers a stop for 1.5 s. Drive commands, recalibration and patrol mode come over Bluetooth.

Mechanical

I designed a 200 × 130 mm deck around four TT-motor mounts, with slotted clamp plates to locate each motor shaft. The 190 mm boom includes height adjustment to place the coil 15–20 mm above the ground. Non-metallic supports and nylon hardware reduce interference near the sensing area.

Coil

38–40 turns of 0.5 mm enamelled wire on a printed 100 mm former, about 300 µH and 1 Ω, with tightly twisted leads under 30 cm and the winding potted so the turns can't move. Moving turns read as false signals.

Mechatronics · BU ME360

Move fast, don't tip the bar

A motor-driven platform that carries an unsupported upright aluminum bar 10 ft out and back as fast as possible without letting it topple.

  • SolidWorks Motion
  • Arduino UNO
  • PWM motor driver
  • 12 V gear motors
  • Laser cutting

I started with a free-body diagram of the bar. Summing forces and moments about its base gives the largest acceleration before the bar rotates off its tipping edge: amax = g·b/L, where b is the base width and L the height. For this bar that came to about g/12, or 0.82 m/s². That number became the design target for everything else.

I modeled the platform in SolidWorks to check weight distribution and motor and wheel mounting, then laser-cut the structure. The bar sits centered between the axles so the tipping moment is the same accelerating and braking. I compared several wheel diameters: larger wheels give more speed but less torque at the ground. I chose 5 in as the balance between acceleration, ground clearance and axle spacing.

Acceleration vs. tippingfind the limit
0.70 m/s²
Bar stays up
Ideal one-way time –Tip limit g/12 ≈ 0.82 m/s²

Electronics

An Arduino UNO drives the 12 V gear motors through a motor driver board. Pins D2 and D3 set direction and D5 and D6 send PWM for speed, with OUT1 and OUT2 driving the motor leads and a shared 5 V and ground reference.

Mechanical

Each motor is held by a laser-cut U-bracket and a locking bar. Support plates with bored openings guide the axles, and the Arduino and driver are screwed to the deck. A belt couples the motor to the drive axle.

Simulation vs. reality

SolidWorks motion study4.3 s one way · 8.6 s round trip
Prototype testing≈ 13 s round trip
In-class trial≈ 15 s, bar stayed up, ran straight

The gap comes from friction, motor inefficiency, uneven torque response and small misalignments that the ideal model leaves out.

Design for manufacturing · CNC machining

Designing parts the machine can actually make

A BU pencil holder I designed in SolidWorks and cut on a CNC machine, plus a machined mounting bracket. In both, every feature was chosen with the tool and the setup in mind.

  • SolidWorks
  • CNC machining
  • Draft angles
  • Tool-radius fillets
  • Engraving

A CAD model can describe shapes a cutter can't produce. Sharp inside corners, walls too thin to hold their shape under cutting load and features the tool can't reach all look fine on screen and fail at the machine. I designed the pencil holder backwards from the process: what the cutter can reach, how the stock is held, and what the part needs to look finished without extra hand work.

Section A–A · pencil holderwhy each feature is there
  • 1Draft on the walls. The taper gives the cutter clean access, takes away undercuts, and reads as a deliberate form instead of a plain tube.
  • 2Inside fillets sized to the cutter. A round end mill can't cut a sharp inside corner, so I set every inside radius at or above the tool radius. That avoids a smaller tool, a slower toolpath and a corner that would never match the model.
  • 3Stepped rim. It breaks the sharp edge at the opening and gives a clean finished lip.
  • 4Engraving sized for a small tool. The BU lettering is shallow and wide enough for an engraving cutter to trace in one pass.
  • 5Edge breaks on the base. Chamfered outer edges remove burrs and sharp corners without a secondary operation.

Machined bracket

The bracket applies the same rules to a functional part: a bored seat with a shoulder to locate a bearing, a four-bolt flange around it, and a base with counterbored mounting holes so the screw heads sit flush.

Stiffness without bulk

An angled gusset ties the upright to the base where the bending moment is highest. Pockets remove material where it carries little load, and every inside corner between the pockets is filleted to suit a standard end mill.

Locating features

A slot on the underside lets the bracket key into its mating part, and a small tapped hole on top allows a set screw or fitting. Both are reachable from standard setups.

A 2.5-axis Cartesian robot that plays a carnival game

A gantry that moves a spring-loaded launcher to set positions and fires a ping pong ball straight up for a player to hit with a Nerf blaster. Three shots per round, with automatic recovery and reload after each miss.

  • SolidWorks assembly
  • Stepper motors
  • Timing belts
  • G-code
  • MATLAB
  • 3D printing

I developed the mechanical design and full assembly in SolidWorks from our team concept, integrating the linear stages, launcher and ball-catching mechanism. We then fabricated and assembled the system using printed components and aluminum extrusion. My design work connected three requirements: precise positioning, controlled energy release and reliable ball recovery.

Operating sequence× 3 per round
  1. Power on and home all stages; ball rests in the cone
  2. Stages drive the launcher to a preset shooting position
  3. Stepper turns the gear train and pulls the rack down
  4. Rubber bands stretch and store elastic energy
  5. The fourth gear reaches its set point and slips; the rack fires the ball up
  6. Player shoots at the ball as it rises and falls
  7. Cone and damping layers catch the ball and settle it to reload
  8. Move to a new position and repeat

Linear stages

Three belt-driven stages, each with a printed stepper mount, an idler pulley support and a moving carriage. The vertical stage rides on the carriages of the first two through a custom printed connector. Belts were tensioned for smooth travel.

Launcher

A stepper drives a four-gear train that pulls a rack down against rubber bands. When the last gear reaches a set point it disengages, the rack slips free, and the stored elastic energy drives it up to launch the ball. MATLAB controlled the loading and release timing.

Catching the ball

A ball hitting rigid plastic bounces out, so a printed cone guides it down onto two paper damping layers: crumpled paper on a flat sheet to absorb impact, and a second paper cone to slow and center it. Each axis was proven out in G-code for direction and travel before full integration.

Follow the load path through an acrylic truss

I designed an acrylic truss bridge in SolidWorks to balance load capacity against material and joint cost. I developed the geometry, analyzed member forces in MATLAB and by hand, and built the structure in acrylic.

  • SolidWorks
  • MATLAB
  • Method of joints
  • Euler buckling
  • Laser-cut acrylic

I wrote a MATLAB joint-equilibrium solver to get every member force, then checked them by hand. That sorted members into tension and compression, and every compression member was checked against buckling. Changing the geometry and re-running showed how load redistributes and where capacity runs out first.

The prototype showed what the model leaves out: joint stiffness, assembly variation and imperfect load application all shift the real structure away from the ideal pin-jointed answer.

Mechanisms · BU ME360

Turning a motor's rotation into a dolphin's tail stroke

I designed the hull and five-bar tail-drive assembly in SolidWorks to turn motor rotation into a sweeping, wave-like stroke. I developed the linkage geometry and packaging together, keeping the mechanism inside the hull while allowing the tail to move through its full range.

  • Five-bar linkage
  • SolidWorks assembly
  • SolidWorks Motion
  • Bio-inspired design

Dolphins push water with an up-and-down tail stroke. I first built a four-bar version to see how the crank, coupler and rocker interact and where the motion runs out. Adding a fifth link gave enough freedom for a smoother, more lifelike sweep.

The motor drives crank A–B. The couplers turn that rotation into a sweep, and with pivots A and D fixed, the outer link moves like a tail. The hull was sized from boat dimensions measured in class, and an open channel through its middle keeps the linkage protected inside the body while the tail keeps its full range of motion.

Design pathfour bars → five bars
  1. Four-bar model to learn the crank–coupler–rocker motion and its limits
  2. Add a fifth link for a smoother, wave-like output path
  3. Skeleton model: crank A–B on the motor, fixed pivots A and D
  4. Size the hull from measured boat dimensions
  5. Open channel through the hull to house and protect the linkage
  6. SolidWorks motion study to verify the tail sweep before building

Mechanisms · BU ME360

Sizing a motor from a four-bar's motion analysis

I designed and assembled a one-degree-of-freedom four-bar linkage in SolidWorks, then used SolidWorks Motion to evaluate its behavior with material properties, gravity and a rotary motor. The analysis connects the geometry I created to the torque, power and bearing loads the drive must handle.

  • Four-bar linkage
  • SolidWorks Motion
  • Graphical synthesis
  • Excel trace data

I set every link to carbon steel and traced three points along the extender link, exporting each path to Excel. The motor torque plot peaks at about 720 N·mm. In parts of the cycle the torque goes negative, meaning gravity and the link geometry are back-driving the motor and returning energy to it.

The crank sweeps almost a full turn, from about +179° to −176°. Bearing 1 carries a peak vertical reaction of about 13 N downward, and the second bearing about 10 N upward with the same curve shape.

Motor sizingP = τ · ω
720 N·mmpeak crank torque
62.83 rad/s600 rpm crank speed
≈ 45 Wpeak mechanical power
≈ 13 Npeak bearing reaction

At the modeled 600 rpm, 0.720 N·m × 62.83 rad/s ≈ 45 W is the peak mechanical power. Motor selection also depends on RMS torque, duty cycle, transmission losses and thermal limits.

Linkage synthesis exercises

I also designed linkages graphically, drawing perpendicular bisectors of a target motion path to place the fixed pivots and set link lengths. One exercise produced a 30° back-and-forth plate motion, and a final design opens and closes a container through every point on its required path.

Thermal systems · Boston University coursework

Where a real chiller loses efficiency

A thermodynamic study of the Trane CGAM-26 air-cooled chiller that cools BU's College of Communication, running on R-410A.

  • Vapor-compression cycle
  • R-410A properties
  • Energy balances
  • Field survey

I identified the compressor, condenser, expansion valve and evaporator on site and mapped them to four refrigerant states. Temperature and pressure data fixed the properties at each state, and energy balances through each component gave cooling capacity, work input and COP.

Widening the heat-exchanger temperature difference from 5 °F to 10 °F cut COP by 18.8%. Both cases sit well below the Carnot limit of 9.78, and the gap comes from compressor irreversibility, finite-ΔT heat transfer and pressure losses.

Design with the whole build in mind

design it · build it · measure it · fix it

I'm a mechanical engineering senior at Boston University, graduating in May 2027. I focus on structural analysis and simulation, backed by hands-on design, GD&T documentation and inspection of production hardware.

At General Dynamics, PACCAR and Sigma Defense I worked with controlled tooling drawings, inspection planning, production constraints and prototype fit. Those jobs taught me to think about how a part will be fabricated, assembled, measured and used before I call the design done.

I like working inside constraints and learning from the people who build and use what I design. My Technology Innovation concentration adds the business side: how an engineering decision becomes a product or a process. I'm looking for full-time mechanical, structural, manufacturing or test engineering roles starting June 2027.
